items.title: Perplexity Computer can run completely local on Mac, with a big caveat
items.content_html:
Perplexity Computer now runs entirely on Apple Silicon Macs, but its recommended RAM requirement is pretty steep and limits actual deployments.

The fully local mode launched October 20 for Perplexity Pro, Max, and Enterprise subscribers. The release builds on April's Personal Computer launch and September's Hybrid Compute update. Personal Computer brought AI automation to native Mac apps, while Hybrid Compute paired local processing with cloud-based reasoning.

Users can now choose to keep an entire task on their Mac or authorize cloud processing when additional capabilities are needed. That is, assuming the minimum requirements are met.

The fully local version of Computer supports Qwen 3.6 and PPLX Pro, a Perplexity-trained version of Qwen. Both models run on the Mac, handling reasoning and coordinating tasks without relying on remote AI servers.

With permission, Computer can work across native apps including Notes, Messages, Mail, and Numbers. Rather than simply generating text, the agent can collect information, modify documents, and complete tasks involving several apps.

Perplexity says Computer can review messages and emails, identify outstanding deadlines, and create a task list in Notes. It can also analyze private financial information against downloaded market data, update an Excel workbook, and prepare a Keynote presentation for review.

Code execution and tool operations take place in isolated sandbox environments, according to Perplexity, with controlled access to files and supported apps. Users can also authorize Computer to access cloud services for current information, browser use, connected apps, and advanced reasoning using more than 15 frontier models.

Fully local processing doesn't necessarily make every workflow independent of the internet. Sending an email or accessing an online service still requires a network connection, even when the AI model itself remains on the Mac.

Perplexity recommends at least 36 GB of unified memory for running Computer locally, which exceeds the maximum available in some recent Apple silicon Macs. According to Apple's technical specifications, the standard M6 Mac mini starts with 16 GB and supports a maximum of 32 GB, falling short of Perplexity's recommendation.

The M5 Pro Mac mini can meet the recommendation with a 48 GB or 64 GB configuration. Meanwhile, the M5 Max Mac Studio starts with 36 GB, making it the less expensive of the two Mac Studio configurations that meets the recommendation without upgrades.

Older Apple Silicon Macs with sufficient memory can also qualify. Perplexity describes 36 GB as a recommendation rather than a strict minimum, so users with less memory aren't necessarily prevented from running the software.

The recommendation illustrates how memory capacity can determine which Macs are suitable for demanding local AI workloads. Larger models need enough space for their data while leaving resources available for macOS and other running apps.

Perplexity previously published inference benchmarks for Qwen 3.6 on an M5 Max MacBook Pro. Those tests don't show how complete Computer workflows perform across different Mac configurations, and Perplexity hasn't released comparable results.

Perplexity's expansion comes as Apple moves to tighten macOS privacy protections against autonomous AI agents. On October 2, Apple announced plans to strengthen Full Disk Access controls to prevent apps from exposing sensitive information without users fully understanding the risks.

Full Disk Access allows backup utilities to reach files that macOS ordinarily protects, but it can also expose emails, messages, browsing history, and other private information. The risks extend to people communicating with the Mac's owner, whose information could become accessible through those apps.

In a developer notice, Apple said future controls will require more explicit user action before granting such extensive access. The company hasn't announced when those changes will arrive, and it isn't eliminating Full Disk Access entirely.

Perplexity says Computer uses controlled permissions and isolated execution environments, but its announcement doesn't specify whether the local agent requires Full Disk Access.

Local AI processing reduces the need to send private data to remote servers, but it doesn't eliminate security risks. An agent can still mishandle sensitive files or follow malicious instructions embedded in documents.

The launch also gives Mac users another alternative to Siri AI, which uses on-device models and Apple's Private Cloud Compute infrastructure for more demanding requests. Both systems can work with personal context and perform actions across apps, although their capabilities and underlying architectures differ.

items.title: Sony's XR patent sale to Meta is a problem for Apple Vision Pro gaming
items.content_html:
Sony sold over 400 XR patents to Meta, which is bad news for the future of VR gaming on PlayStation. It will become a problem for Apple Vision Pro gamers.

The sale of patents between companies isn't a new phenomenon, but sometimes they have unintended side effects. In the case of patent transfers from Sony to Meta, it's a move that will impact Apple down the road.

In early October, as first reported by ZD Net Korea and translated by Road to VR, Sony sold a collection of 419 XR-related patents to Meta. After signing a Confirmatory Assignment agreement in December 2025, batches of patents were transferred from Sony to Meta.

The portfolio consisted of 180 U.S. patents and 239 patent-family filings, the latter being filed in other regions. Those patents covered a variety of topics, including processing for XR applications, head-mounted display designs, and other related hardware.

Neither Sony nor Meta has officially announced anything about the deal or transfers, nor has Sony discussed future VR hardware ambitions.

That said, supplies of the PlayStation VR 2 have been tight for months. Production of the headset and controllers has reportedly ended.

Patent transfers are sometimes a worry for companies that have to regularly deal with infringement lawsuits. For once, the problem here isn't as severe as that where Apple is concerned.

More, it's one about game controls on the Apple Vision Pro, and the company's future plans in that area.

In June 2025, reports revealed that PlayStation VR2 controller support was coming to the Apple Vision Pro as part of visionOS 26. By November 2025, you can also buy the controllers from Apple directly for $249.95.

PS VR2 controllers used with an Apple Vision Pro - Image Credit: Apple

Adding support for the PS VR2 controllers solved a small problem for Apple. It made the Apple Vision Pro more capable of gaming.

Apple designed the Apple Vision Pro to be primarily controlled by your voice and hand gestures. However, the vast majority of games in the VR space rely on some form of handheld controller, not a hand-tracking system.

By adding that support, Apple inherited an existing game controller system that works well, designed by a company with a long history in gaming. If Apple was going to support controllers from any company, it would be the one with massive gaming credentials.

The PS VR2 controllers were also stylish and mainly white, which also fit Apple's preferred color scheme.

The controllers are not a completely dead product yet, but the warning signs are there. Retail stock is dwindling.

The patent trade doesn't mean anything in a legal sense for the Apple Vision Pro just now. Supply will be an issue soon.

It means Apple has to think twice about any future decisions regarding VR controllers. Especially when Sony eventually decides to stop supplying them because its exhausted its stockpile.

The obvious way forward is for Apple to make it easier for third-party game controller manufacturers to support the Apple Vision Pro. It already supports practically any standard game controller on the market, so doing the same for VR isn't a massive stretch of the imagination

If there's another pair of suitable controllers being sold in the future by a major gaming company, Apple will seek to work with it instead.

A third way is for Apple to go it alone with its own VR game controllers. Code references in September revealed that there are two game controllers in development within Apple, though the more traditional type and not VR.

It's already doing the development work for a product that gets Apple halfway there. Going all the way is always an option, if it can stomach the increase in research and development costs.

items.title: iPhone Duo delivery dates stabilize on late January deliveries for all models
items.content_html:
If you missed out on getting your iPhone Duo Friday morning, you likely won't see yours show up until early 2027. At least is isn't getting worse anymore.

On Friday, Apple opened preorders for the iPhone Duo, its first foldable. Announced in September, the buzz following the event left little doubt that it would be an immediate hit.

And that certainly seems to be the case. The iPhone Duo sold out almost immediately, with dates slipping into late November and early December within moments of preorders opening.

As of Friday afternoon, the iPhone Duo dates have slipped into late January. That holds regardless of storage size or color, suggesting that demand is equal across configuration or supply numbers are low.

iPhone Duo delivery dates have been pushed into January

Apple never states how many devices it has made ready for sale on day one, but the shipping dates normally provide a clue as to whether a model is a hit.

Carriers had stock until later in the process. AT&T and Verizon had same-week delivery until about noon. Best Buy had a two-week shipment for most models as late as 2PM ET on October 16.

Supply from the carriers seems to fluctuate, though, and they tend to over-promise and under-deliver. Apple is more conservative with under-promising and shipping early, in most cases

For those who want to try their luck in brick-and-mortar stores, the iPhone Duo will be available to purchase in-store on October 23. You should expect increased crowd sizes and lines, though, and going to an Apple Store does not mean you'll leave with an iPhone Duo, either.

items.title: iPhone Duo sells out moments after pre-orders begin
items.content_html:
As expected, Apple's iPhone Duo has seen shipping slip back in most configurations instantly.

Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo began at 8 A.M. Eastern and as with most new iPhones — but not all — the stocks sold out rapidly. With the first moments, shipping dates slipped back to November 16, and then to November 23, for all configurations.

Apple never states how many devices it has made ready for sale on day one, but the shipping dates normally provide a clue as to whether a model is a hit.

In this case, that's less apparent than usual because there is another factor. Alongside demand from early buyers, it's believed that Apple has fewer of the iPhone Duo manufactured than normal.

That could be because of the many reports of delays in manufacturing over such a complex new design. But there is also the fact that this is a new design and so demand may have proven harder to estimate.

Then, too, the iPhone Duo is the most expensive iPhone ever made. It's also launching at a time when the global chip shortage has driven all technology prices higher.

You will still be able to place an order for the iPhone Duo, you just won't get it when the first shipments begin on October 23. However, that same date is when the iPhone Duo will be in stores, and those stores will have at least some stocks.

items.title: Generative AI porn apps targeted in App Review Guidelines update
items.content_html:
Apple has updated the App Review Guidelines once more, in a crackdown on apps creating non-consensual adult imagery that are sold using bait-and-switch tactics to pass the review process.

While Apple has a fairly robust App Store Review process and guidelines to match, not everything that makes it through the examination does so legitimately. In some cases, developers use deceitful tactics to hide an app's true nature so it can get into the App Store, despite having features that are against the rules.

Bait-and-switch apps that present as one thing to the App Store but can be something quite different aren't new. This behavior has been used by scam and malicious apps, as well as, in one instance, Russian banks.

In the latest crackdown, Apple's Developer site outlines why a set of changes have been made to the App Review Guidelines. The news post, issued late on October 16, explains it is a change against "nonconsensual intimate imagery and bait-and-switch apps."

Apps with pornographic material have long been prohibited by the App Store, including those that generate sexually explicit images. This includes "nudification" apps that generate explicit images of real people using photos supplied by the user, without the subject's consent.

In July, Apple was ordered to remove eight such iPhone apps from the App Store by the city of San Francisco.

Apps with user-generated content also have a requirement to filter objectionable material, including allowing users to report such content, and to allow users to block accounts.

As part of the changes, Apple adds that apps with hidden or undocumented features are also not allowed on the App Store. This includes apps that "misrepresent their purpose during review, and only reveal their harmful capabilities after it's approved.

1.2: Content moderation requirements now say that apps should proactively prevent or remove content with non-consensual intimate imagery, including those made using AI generation tools.

Rule 2.5.19 clarifies Apple's stance on banning apps with bait-and-switch tactics affecting the App Store Review process.

Though Apple has long prevented apps that enable human trafficking or the exploitation of children in the App Store, Section 5 clarifies the stance. Apps found to facilitate these actions will be removed from the App Store and blocked from "alternative distribution."
